title: Delhi Just Banned New Petrol Two-Wheelers From 2028. The Capital's ₹15,000 Crore EV Gamble Is Now Live.
excerpt: India's most polluted major city has launched its most aggressive electric vehicle policy yet, offering full tax waivers, scrappage cash, and a hard deadline to phase out internal combustion engines for key vehicle categories.
body:
Starting this week, anyone buying a battery-powered car in Delhi under ₹30 lakh pays zero road tax and zero registration fees. Anyone scrapping an old petrol car for an EV gets up to ₹1 lakh in cash. And by April 2028, the capital will stop registering new petrol and CNG two-wheelers entirely.

The Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy 2026, notified on July 1 and backed by a ₹15,000 crore investment over four years, is the most aggressive state-level EV mandate India has ever seen. It sets a target that sounds almost utopian for a city where auto-rickshaws still run on compressed natural gas and two-stroke scooters crowd every intersection: 95 percent of all new vehicle registrations must be electric by 2027.

## What the Policy Actually Does

The policy, approved by the Delhi Cabinet under Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on June 29, runs until March 31, 2030. It operates on three levers: incentives, infrastructure, and mandates.

**Incentives** are front-loaded to drive early adoption. Electric two-wheeler buyers receive ₹30,000 in the first year, declining to ₹10,000 by year three. Electric auto-rickshaws get up to ₹50,000. Small electric commercial trucks (N1 category, under 3.5 tonnes) get up to ₹1 lakh. All disbursements flow through Direct Benefit Transfer — no middlemen, no dealer markups.

The scrappage programme, backed by more than ₹1,500 crore, targets the oldest and dirtiest vehicles. Owners of BS-IV and earlier cars registered before April 2020 can trade them in for an EV and pocket up to ₹1 lakh. Two-wheeler scrappage pays ₹10,000, three-wheelers ₹25,000.

**Infrastructure** is where the money concentrates. The government plans over 30,000 public EV charging points across the city — a dramatic expansion from the current base. This is a recognition that range anxiety, not price, remains the single biggest barrier to EV adoption in Indian cities.

**Mandates** are the policy's sharpest teeth. From January 1, 2027, Delhi will register only electric auto-rickshaws and N1 goods carriers — no new CNG or petrol registrations in those categories. From April 1, 2028, the same applies to two-wheelers. Existing vehicles are not affected, but the new-registration ban effectively forces the market to pivot.

## What's Notably Absent

Hybrid vehicles are excluded. Unlike the draft policy released in April, the final version provides no subsidies or incentives for hybrids, including plug-in hybrids. The government is betting on a full battery-electric future, not a transitional one. That's a blow to Maruti Suzuki and Toyota, which have invested heavily in hybrid technology for the Indian market, and a boost to pure-EV players like Tata Motors, Mahindra, Ather Energy, TVS Motor, and Bajaj Auto.

There's also a three-year lock-in: anyone receiving a government EV subsidy cannot re-register their vehicle in another state for three years. That's designed to prevent subsidy arbitrage — buying cheap in Delhi and registering elsewhere.

## Can Delhi Actually Pull This Off?

The ambition is enormous, but the obstacles are real.

Delhi's current public charging infrastructure is sparse. The 30,000-charging-point target is more than ten times the existing count. Building that out in four years requires not just government spending but private participation — land allocation for charging hubs, grid upgrades to handle the load, and standardisation across charging providers.

Supply chain dependence on China is the elephant in the room. India's EV battery ecosystem remains heavily reliant on Chinese cell imports. Puneet Gupta, an auto analyst, noted that while the pollution case for EVs is strong, "charging infrastructure, supply chains, and China dependence remain key hurdles."

And the ₹15,000 crore commitment is aspirational. Delhi's actual budget allocation for the policy's first year has not been publicly broken down. State EV policies in India have a mixed track record: Delhi's own 2020 EV policy set ambitious targets but fell short on infrastructure delivery.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

Delhi is India's political capital and its second-largest auto market. Where Delhi goes, other states watch. If this policy succeeds, it will accelerate EV mandates across India's major metros, creating a market that Goldman Sachs has projected could reach 10 million EVs annually by 2030.

For NRIs, the investment case is direct. India's EV charging infrastructure needs an estimated $10 billion in capital over the next decade. Companies like Tata Power, Adani Total Gas, and a growing roster of startups (Ather, Exponent Energy, Kazam) are raising capital to build out networks. Delhi's policy provides the demand-side certainty that makes those investments underwritable.

The policy also matters to the millions of NRIs who return to Delhi regularly. A cleaner, quieter city — with lower particulate pollution from two-stroke engines — is a quality-of-life improvement that resonates beyond investment returns.

"No state in the country has provided this level of support for EV adoption," Chief Minister Gupta said at the policy's announcement. Whether that support translates into transformation will depend on execution. The clock is now running.
